headline: Monhegan Ledges Give Up Pollock and Cod While Bass Push Deep Into Penobscot Bay
subhead: Cool Gulf of Maine water is keeping stripers feeding in daylight while groundfish hold tight to the ledges and channel edges.
body_markdown:
Forty-some years ago my father told me something I still repeat to every greenhorn who steps on my boat: "The bay doesn't lie, but it doesn't hurry to tell you the truth either." I thought about that Tuesday morning hauling gear off White Head, watching a school of pollock roll bait right on the surface not thirty yards from the buoy — something I hadn't seen that thick in years. My sternman, twenty-two and new to this, wanted to drop everything and go get a rod. I told him to finish the string first. The pollock weren't going anywhere. That's the kind of week it's been — steady, unhurried, and if you pay attention, generous.

Striped bass have been the story up and down the bay, and the reason is simple: our water hasn't warmed the way it has south of Cape Cod. Down there the bass have gone nocturnal, sliding off the flats at first light and not showing again till dusk. Up here, with Gulf of Maine water still running cool, the fish are willing to feed right through the middle of the day. I've been finding schoolies to 28 inches working the pinch points at Eggemoggin Reach on the last two hours of the flood, and better fish — a few pushing 34, 35 inches — holding off the ledges at Eastern Egg Rock where the mackerel and pogies have been stacking up thick enough to color the water. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, or a 2-ounce white bucktail worked slow along the rip, has been the ticket. The puffins are still working that same bait up there, which tells you all you need to know about how much forage is sitting on that ledge right now.

Rockland breakwater has been a reliable mackerel spot again this week — small jigs, no bait needed, tight to the rocks on the last of the outgoing. Bring a few extra Sabikis because the mackerel are running with a scattering of pollock underneath them, and those pollock will happily take a jig meant for something smaller. Boothbay Harbor's had the same pattern just inside the islands, mackerel thick enough that the charter boats have been filling bait wells in twenty minutes flat before running offshore.

Groundfish have been the quieter but more consistent part of the week. Cod are holding deep in the Penobscot Bay channels — 90 to 120 feet off the eastern side between Vinalhaven and North Haven, and out toward the deeper water past Matinicus. Jigging diamond jigs or bouncing a whole clam bait on a high-low rig near bottom has produced fish in the 20-to-25-inch range, nothing enormous but steady enough to make a morning worthwhile. Haddock have been mixed in with that same crowd, though you have to work for them — smaller fish, and you'll cull through some shorts. Monhegan remains the most dependable groundfish stop in the zone. The ledges on the northeast side, particularly on the ebb when the current sets up clean against the rock, have been giving up both cod and pollock, with the pollock often willing to hit right up near the surface on a slow retrieve with a soft-plastic swimbait — the same fish my sternman wanted to chase off White Head.

Bluefish haven't shown in any real numbers up this way yet, which isn't unusual for us — that's still mostly a southern New England story right now, with the big blitzes running from the Jersey shore into Raritan Bay. We flagged last week that bluefish would keep following bunker up the coast as long as the weather held calm and stable, and that's exactly what's happened south of us — the bite has spread, just not quite into Maine water yet. If it keeps pushing north the way it has, don't be surprised if we start seeing a few stray blues mixed in around Casco Bay by early August. I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet, but it's worth watching.

Tide and moon matter more than usual right now. We're rolling toward a first-quarter phase, which means the current is easing off peak strength through the Reach and around Stonington's tighter passages. That's actually good news for bass fishing — a softer current means longer, more comfortable feeding windows instead of a narrow slack-tide scramble, and it should widen the productive stretch on both the Eggemoggin and Fox Islands Thorofare drifts through the next several days.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the southwest and light like it has been, I'd put my time into the Eastern Egg Rock bass and the Monhegan groundfish — both have been the most consistent producers of the summer so far. If a northeast blow comes through and stirs up the outer ledges, shift inside to the bay channels off Vinalhaven where the cod have been holding regardless of surface conditions. Best case, this cool-water pattern holds and the bass keep feeding through daylight for another few weeks before the summer heat finally catches up to us. Worst case, a hot stretch pushes them into the same low-light pattern they're running south of us — but up here, that's usually a late-August problem, not a late-July one.
